children.label: b

answer.short: True; the list runs from 0 to 999 999 and ends.
answer.worked: True. The set is $\{0,1,2,\ldots,999\,999\}$ and contains exactly $1\,000\,000$ elements, so it is finite.

children.label: c
children.prompt: $\{\text{human beings who have ever lived}\}$ is an infinite set.

answer.short: False; only finitely many human beings have lived up to now.
answer.worked: False. At the present time, the total number of human beings who have lived is finite, even though it is very large.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If two finite sets are equal, then they have the same number of elements.

answer.short: True; equal sets have exactly the same elements.
answer.worked: True. Equal sets contain exactly the same distinct elements, so counting their elements gives the same number.

children.prompt: If two finite sets have the same number of elements, then they are equal.

answer.short: False; for example, $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ each have one element but are unequal.

answer.short: True; both sets have no elements.
answer.worked: True. Both sets have exactly the same elements—none—so they are equal. There is only one empty set.

content.prompt: Explain why each statement below is true.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If $S$ is a set, then $\varnothing\subseteq S$.

answer.short: The empty set has no element outside $S$, so $\varnothing\subseteq S$.
answer.worked: A subset must have all its elements in $S$. The empty set has no elements, so it has no element outside $S$. Therefore $\varnothing\subseteq S$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If $A\subseteq B$ and $B\subseteq C$, then $A\subseteq C$.

answer.short: Every element of $A$ belongs to $B$, and hence to $C$.
answer.worked: Every element of $A$ is in $B$. Every element of $B$ is in $C$, so every element of $A$ is also in $C$. Therefore $A\subseteq C$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If $S$ is a set, then $S\subseteq S$.

answer.worked: Every element of $S$ is an element of $S$ itself, which satisfies the definition of a subset. Therefore $S\subseteq S$.

answer.short: Each set contains every element of the other, so they have exactly the same elements.
answer.worked: Since $A\subseteq B$, every element of $A$ is in $B$. Since $B\subseteq A$, every element of $B$ is in $A$. Thus the sets have exactly the same elements, so $A=B$.

answer.short: The only element of $\{x\}$ is $x$, which belongs to $S$.
answer.worked: The set $\{x\}$ has only one element, $x$. Since $x\in S$, every element of $\{x\}$ is in $S$. Therefore $\{x\}\subseteq S$.

children.label: f
children.prompt: If $x\in S$ and $y\in S$, then $\{x,y\}\subseteq S$.

answer.worked: Each element of $\{x,y\}$ is either $x$ or $y$. Both belong to $S$, so every element of $\{x,y\}$ is in $S$. Therefore $\{x,y\}\subseteq S$.

children.label: g
children.prompt: If $A\subseteq B$, where $A$ and $B$ are finite sets, then $|A|\leq|B|$.

answer.short: $B$ contains every element of $A$, so it has at least as many elements as $A$.
answer.worked: Every element of $A$ belongs to $B$. Thus $B$ contains all the elements counted in $|A|$, and may contain more. Since the sets are finite, $|A|\leq|B|$.

answer.worked: A set is a subset of itself. For example, let $A=B=\{1\}$. Then $A\subseteq B$, but $|A|=|B|=1$, so $|A|<|B|$ is false.

children.prompt: If $A=B$ and $A$ and $B$ are finite sets, then $|A|=|B|$.

answer.short: True; equal sets have the same elements.
answer.worked: Since $A=B$, the sets contain exactly the same elements. Counting those elements gives $|A|=|B|$, so the statement is true.

children.prompt: If $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ and $A$, $B$ and $C$ are finite sets, then $|A|\leq |C|$.

answer.short: True; $C$ contains every element of $A$ and may contain more.
answer.worked: Every element of $A$ belongs to $B$, and every element of $B$ belongs to $C$. Thus every element of $A$ belongs to $C$. Since the sets are finite, $C$ has at least as many elements as $A$, so $|A|\leq |C|$.

content.prompt: Explain why the following statements are true, where $A$ and $B$ are any two sets.

answer.short: Every element of $A\cap B$ belongs to $A$.
answer.worked: The intersection $A\cap B$ contains only elements belonging to both $A$ and $B$. Every one of these elements therefore belongs to $A$, so $A\cap B\subseteq A$.

answer.short: Every element of $A\cap B$ belongs to $B$.
answer.worked: The intersection $A\cap B$ contains only elements belonging to both $A$ and $B$. Every one of these elements therefore belongs to $B$, so $A\cap B\subseteq B$.

answer.short: The union $A\cup B$ contains every element of $A$.
answer.worked: The union $A\cup B$ contains all elements belonging to $A$ or $B$, including those belonging to both. Thus every element of $A$ belongs to $A\cup B$, so $A\subseteq A\cup B$.

answer.short: Every element common to $A$ and $B$ also belongs to their union.
answer.worked: An element of $A\cap B$ belongs to both $A$ and $B$. The union $A\cup B$ includes elements belonging to either set or both sets. Hence every element of $A\cap B$ belongs to $A\cup B$, so $A\cap B\subseteq A\cup B$.

answer.short: The empty set is a subset of every set, including $A\cap B$.
answer.worked: The empty set has no elements, so it has no element outside $A\cap B$. It is therefore a subset of $A\cap B$.

answer.short: The empty set is a subset of every set, including $A\cup B$.
answer.worked: The empty set has no elements, so it has no element outside $A\cup B$. It is therefore a subset of $A\cup B$.

content.prompt: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are finite sets. Are the following statements true or false? Explain your answers.

answer.short: True. $A\cup\varnothing=A$, so their numbers of elements are equal.
answer.worked: The empty set contributes no elements to the union, so $A\cup\varnothing=A$. Therefore $|A\cup\varnothing|=|A|$, and the statement is true.
No element belongs to the empty set, so there are no elements common to $A$ and $\varnothing$. Thus $A\cap\varnothing=\varnothing$ and $|A\cap\varnothing|=0$. The statement is true.

answer.short: False. For example, if $A=B=\{1\}$, then $|A\cup B|=1$ but $|A|+|B|=2$.
answer.worked: Take $A=B=\{1\}$. Then $A\cup B=\{1\}$, so $|A\cup B|=1$, whereas $|A|+|B|=1+1=2$. Since $1\ne2$, the statement is false. Adding the two set sizes counts their common element twice.

answer.short: False. For example, if $A=B=\{1\}$, then $|A\cap B|=1$ but $|A|-|B|=0$.
answer.worked: Take $A=B=\{1\}$. Then $A\cap B=\{1\}$, so $|A\cap B|=1$, whereas $|A|-|B|=1-1=0$. Since $1\ne0$, this counterexample shows that the statement is false.

content.prompt:
In all of the following, $E$ stands for the universal set.

State whether each statement is true or false. Explain your answers.

answer.worked: The complement of $A^c$ contains exactly the elements of $E$ that are not outside $A$. These are the elements of $A$, so $(A^c)^c=A$. The statement is true.

answer.short: True; every element of $E$ is either in $A$ or in $A^c$.
answer.worked: Every element of $E$ is either in $A$ or not in $A$. The latter elements form $A^c$, so their union contains all of $E$. Thus $A\cup A^c=E$, and the statement is true.
No element can be both in $A$ and not in $A$. Therefore $A$ and $A^c$ have no elements in common: $A\cap A^c=\varnothing$. The statement is false.
The complement is taken within $E$. There are no elements of $E$ outside $E$, so $E^c=\varnothing$. The statement is false.

answer.short: True; every element of $E$ is outside the empty set.
answer.worked: The empty set contains no elements. Consequently every element of $E$ belongs to its complement, so $\varnothing^c=E$. The statement is true.

answer.short: False. For example, if $E=\{1,2,3\}$ and $A=\{1\}$, then $|A|=1$ and $|A^c|=2$.
answer.worked: Take $E=\{1,2,3\}$ and $A=\{1\}$. Then $A^c=\{2,3\}$, so $|A|=1$ and $|A^c|=2$. These cardinalities differ, providing a counterexample. The statement is false.

A set is just a collection of objects, but we need some new words, symbols and diagrams to be able to talk sensibly about sets. Some tricky counting problems can be solved by using a type of diagram called a Venn diagram to illustrate the sets involved.

The symbols ∈ and ∉
The phrase ‘is an element of’ occurs so often in discussing sets that the special symbol ∈ is used for it. For example, if A = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then 3 ∈ A. (We read ‘3 ∈ A’ as ‘3 is an element of the set A’.)
The symbol ∉ means ‘is not an element of’. For example, if A = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then 8 ∉ A. (We read ‘8 ∉ A’ as ‘8 is not an element of the set A’.)

• If a is an element of a set S, we write a ∈ S.
• If b is not an element of a set S, we write b ∉ S.

Venn diagrams
Diagrams make mathematics easier because they help us to see the whole situation at a glance. The English mathematician John Venn (1834–1923) began using diagrams to represent sets. These diagrams are now called Venn diagrams.

entries.description:
The universal set
In most problems involving sets, it is convenient to choose a larger set that contains all of the elements in all of the sets being considered. There will usually be a natural choice of such a set. This larger set is called the universal set, and is usually given the symbol E. In a Venn diagram, the universal set is generally drawn as a rectangle, and then subsets of E are represented by circles within this rectangle.

entries.description:
Set complements and Venn diagrams
• We often choose a natural universal set that contains all the elements under discussion.
• The complement of a particular set consists of all elements of the universal set that are not in the set under discussion.
• Sets are represented in a Venn diagram by circles inside the universal set.
• The overlapping region of two circles represents the intersection of the two sets, and the two circles together represent their union.
• When two sets are known to be disjoint, the circles are drawn without any overlap.
• When one set is known to be a subset of another, its circle is drawn inside the circle of the other set.
